opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. What I find most remarkable is that it works at all, in the sense that people didn't think it was possible. For years the assumption was that every predictive problem on enterprise data needed its own pipeline: you take your relational database with customers, transactions, products, and so on, and a data scientist spends weeks or months on feature engineering, joining tables, aggregating, and then training a model for that one task. Churn is one model, fraud is another, recommendations are another.

With a relational foundation model, you point it at a database it has never seen, with a schema it has never seen, ask a predictive question like "which customers are likely to churn in the next 30 days?" or "what will this user buy next?", and it gives you an accurate prediction in about a second, with no task-specific training. That's in-context learning, the same idea that made large language models so powerful, applied to structured relational data.

The key insight is to treat the database as a graph. Each row is a node, and primary-key/foreign-key relationships are edges. Once you see it that way, you can build a model that reasons over the whole relational structure, not a single flattened table, and you can pretrain it on lots of diverse databases so it learns general patterns of how relational data behaves: how recency matters, how behavior propagates across entities, how temporal dynamics work.

What surprised us is how competitive this zero-shot approach is with models carefully hand-built by experts, and that if you fine-tune it on your specific data, it typically does better still. So you get a strong prediction in seconds and a top-performing model with a little extra effort. For me that changes the economics of machine learning in the enterprise. Predictive modeling stops being a months-long project and becomes something closer to writing a query.

r001.rationale: The response says the model can answer predictive questions on a database and schema it has never seen, with accurate predictions and no task-specific training.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me, Sam. What I find most remarkable is really a single, almost surprising fact: the model works on databases it has never seen before, with zero training, and it gets accuracy that's competitive with, and often better than, what a data scientist would build by hand over weeks.

Let me step back and explain why that matters. If you look at how predictive machine learning is done in enterprises today, most of the valuable data doesn't live in text or images. It lives in relational databases: customers, orders, transactions, products, events, all spread across dozens or hundreds of tables linked by foreign keys. The way we've done ML on that data for twenty years is that a data scientist sits down, flattens everything into one big table, hand-engineers features, like "number of purchases in the last thirty days," "average order value," and so on, and then trains a gradient-boosted tree. Every new question means a new flattening, a new feature pipeline, a new model. It's slow, expensive, and brittle.

What we did is treat the database itself as the input. You can think of a relational database as a graph: rows are nodes, foreign key links are edges, and time stamps give it a temporal structure. So we built a graph transformer that operates directly on that structure. And then the key move, which is analogous to what happened with language models, is that we pretrained it across many different databases with different schemas, different column names, different numbers of tables, so that it learns a general notion of how entities relate and how histories predict futures.

And then the remarkable thing is what happens when you point it at a new database. You don't retrain. You don't engineer features. You essentially write a query that defines the predictive task, like "for each customer, will they churn in the next ninety days," and the model produces predictions in seconds. In our evaluations, both on public benchmarks and on real customer databases, the zero-shot performance is right up there with the best supervised models, which took teams significant effort to build. And if you give it even a little bit of in-context examples, it gets better still.

I think that's the thing that makes me excited. Foundation models have transformed what you can do with text, with images, with code. But structured, relational data is arguably the most important data asset most organizations have, and it has been left out of that revolution. The idea that you could have a single pretrained model that just understands your database, the way a language model understands a document, and that any analyst could ask a predictive question and get an answer without a six-week ML project, that feels like a genuine shift in how this kind of work gets done.

r001.rationale: The response says the model works on previously unseen databases with zero training and can answer a query defining a predictive task, with competitive accuracy.

astra-6.text:
What I find remarkable is the possibility of learning across relational databases, rather than building a separate model for every prediction task. A lot of enterprise data lives in tables, but the information you need is often in the relationships between those tables. A customer connects to transactions, transactions connect to products, and those connections give you context that you don’t get from looking at a single row.

Traditionally, somebody has to turn that context into features by hand. The exciting idea with a relational foundation model is that it can learn how to use that structure and transfer what it has learned to a new task. You move from asking, “How do I engineer a dataset for this model?” toward asking, “What do I want to predict?” That’s a very different way of making machine learning useful.

r001.rationale: The response says the model can transfer what it has learned to a new task, but does not claim accurate predictions on any database and predictive task without additional model training.

sol-6.1.text:
What I find remarkable is that we can learn directly from the relationships in a database. In most enterprise settings, the data isn’t one nice, flat table. You have customers, transactions, products, and all these connections between them. Traditionally, a data scientist has to figure out how to join those tables and engineer features for each prediction task.

With a relational foundation model, the idea is to learn from that connected structure and transfer what the model has learned to new tasks and new databases. So you can ask, for example, which customer is likely to buy something, or which transaction might be risky, without rebuilding the entire machine-learning pipeline each time.

To me, the exciting part is the possibility of making predictive machine learning much more accessible: letting the model do more of the work that previously required substantial, task-specific human effort.

r001.rationale: The response says the model can transfer to new tasks and databases and may avoid rebuilding the pipeline, but it does not claim accurate predictions on any database and task without additional model training.
